Plan measurement conditions with a D-study

Source: R/api-gstudy-entry.R, R/api-multivariate-gtheory.R
mfrm_d_study.Rd

Would adding tasks or raters make assessment scores more dependable? Use an estimated G-study to compare specified future designs for individual score components and optional weighted composites. Each scenario reports dependability and measurement error for mean scores over common random measurement conditions, such as tasks, raters, or occasions. Projection from an estimated G-study does not refit. Supplying an MFRM first estimates the separate main-effects G-study described below.

Usage 

mfrm_d_study(x, design_grid = NULL, ...)

# Default S3 method
mfrm_d_study(x, design_grid = NULL, ...)

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_multivariate_gstudy'
mfrm_d_study(
  x,
  design_grid = NULL,
  weights = NULL,
  negative_components = c("raw", "genova_algorithm", "genova_ems"),
  ...
)

# S3 method for class 'mfrm_multivariate_d_study'
print(x, digits = NULL, row.names = FALSE, ...)

Arguments

x

A result from mfrm_g_study(). A main-effects result from mfrm_generalizability() or a fitted MFRM uses the separate main-effects method, with its collapsed-residual assumptions. Dispatch preserves the source model; it does not select a new estimator.

design_grid

A nonempty data frame or named list with one positive integer count column per G-study facet. Both G-study routes accept the exact facet label or n_<facet>, such as n_Rater and n_Task. Existing saved count-column names are also accepted: with the rater/task interface, use Raters and/or Tasks for the included facets. With facets, use its exact labels, for example Rater and Occasion for facets = c(Rater = "Assessor", Occasion = "Session"). The mapping is available in x$design$count_columns. Supply exactly one column per facet; extra columns, duplicate aliases and ambiguous matches are refused. Output keeps the saved count-column names, so existing plot and interval selections retain their meaning. Each row is one future complete balanced design preserving the G-study's crossed or nested structure. For nesting = c(Rater = "Task"), Raters means raters per task, not the total rater pool. NULL uses the G-study counts (children per parent for a nested facet) only when its retained data are complete and balanced; incomplete or unequal designs require an explicit grid. Counts need not match or exceed the G-study counts. Conditions are shared across persons and scores in every scenario.

...

Arguments for the selected method. The fitted-MFRM method accepts arguments to mfrm_generalizability(); already estimated G-studies reject unused arguments. Printing accepts arguments for its coefficient table.

weights

Optional named numeric vector for one composite, or a numeric matrix for several named composites. A vector must name every original score exactly once; matrix rows must name every score exactly once, and columns must have unique, nonempty composite names. Rows are matched by name, regardless of order. Every weight must be finite and each composite must have at least one nonzero weight. Signed weights allow difference scores, for example c(Content = 1, Organization = -1). Weights are used as supplied, without normalization. NULL reports original scores only. Otherwise, each scenario reports the original scores once, followed by each composite. A vector's composite is named "Composite"; a matrix preserves its column names and order.

negative_components

Component treatment for D-study point projections. "raw" (default) retains the original estimates. "genova_algorithm" replaces negative variance components with zero; "genova_ems" first recalculates components by source-design expected-mean-square equations, substituting zero as each negative component is encountered. The latter choices require a complete balanced univariate ANOVA G-study with one or two supported crossed or nested random facets. Original G-study estimates remain unchanged. These options do not supply adjusted-estimator intervals.

digits

Display precision passed to the printed tables; NULL uses R's current setting. Stored estimates are unchanged.

row.names

Logical; print table row names? Defaults to FALSE.

Value

An mfrm_multivariate_d_study list containing coefficients (scenario, counts of included facets, score/composite identity, universe/relative/absolute variances under the selected treatment, G/Phi, relative/absolute SEM, ComponentTreatment, and row and metric-specific status, and ComponentPSD), covariances (three matrices per scenario), design_grid, weights (the supplied vector or matrix, reordered to the G-study score order), component_diagnostics, negative_components, effective_components, effective_component_diagnostics, and gstudy (the unchanged source result). summary() returns coefficients. print() returns the same D-study invisibly without computing intervals. summary.mfrm_multivariate_d_study() with intervals = TRUE explicitly calculates and collects supported intervals, methods and source context. print() also shows source level/row counts, future-plan conventions and the supplied composite weights. Save the full result with saveRDS(d) and reopen with readRDS() to preserve that context. A CSV of summary(d) contains the coefficient table only; accompany it with the weights, source design and row usage, future design and score convention. Main-effects inputs instead retain their mfrm_d_study data-frame result; see mfrm_d_study_main_effects for its fields and limitations.

Details

Start with a concrete comparison, such as six versus twelve tasks for every examinee. Each row of design_grid is one scenario. With both facets, data.frame(Raters = c(2, 4), Tasks = c(3, 3)) compares two versus four raters at three tasks; expand.grid(Raters = c(2, 4), Tasks = c(3, 6)) requests all four combinations. These counts apply to every person and score, not to the total number of observed ratings. For facets = c(Rater = "Assessor", Occasion = "Session"), use expand.grid(Rater = c(1, 2), Occasion = c(2, 4)). The same workflow applies to any supported one- or two-facet model; extra columns cannot introduce conditions absent from the G-study.

This is the primary D-study entry for one or several scores. It replaces the public mfrm_multivariate_d_study() name without changing its result class, component estimates, projections or uncertainty methods. For either source model, summary(d) returns its full-precision coefficient table. Optional interval summaries remain specific to the interaction-component route. Main-effects projections do not acquire those interval methods.

Read summary(d) together with plot(d):

  • G concerns consistency of relative ordering, such as ranking examinees. It is not the probability of identifying the best person or the winner of a competition. Close leading scores can remain hard to distinguish even when G is high; this function provides no Person-rank intervals.

  • Phi concerns absolute score levels and also counts shifts from easier tasks or more lenient raters as error. It is not pass/fail accuracy.

  • RelativeSEM and AbsoluteSEM express these errors in the units of the mean score or composite. Smaller SEMs mean less error. They are not confidence intervals for G or Phi.

Larger G/Phi and smaller SEM indicate greater dependability under the model. There is no universally acceptable coefficient: consider the use of scores, consequences of error, and workload before choosing a design. Compare a chosen score/composite and metric across feasible plans. For example, data.frame(Raters = c(2, 3, 4), Tasks = c(6, 4, 3)) holds the number of ratings per person at twelve. It does not hold examinee task burden or total cost constant. The largest projected coefficient is a point-estimate ranking, not evidence that one plan is reliably better. Consider the size of the projected difference and which differences would matter for the assessment. Small rank changes need not imply large practical losses. If a metric is unavailable for any candidate, comparing only the remaining values does not resolve the full planning question. plot(d, type = "sem") shows the SEMs. Plots select a sole composite by default, or the first score when there are no composites. With several composites, specify one with plot(d, composite = "Equal"); use plot(d, score = "V") to inspect an original score named V. The title metadata identifies the plotted score and any composite weights; it is returned with the plot, with titles and notes omitted from the figure by default. Check GStatus, PhiStatus, RelativeSEMStatus, and AbsoluteSEMStatus: each explains the corresponding metric's availability. NA means unavailable, not zero dependability. ComponentPSD separately flags covariance components needing review. See plot.mfrm_multivariate_d_study() for interpreting curves and unavailable estimates.

For a balanced one-facet ANOVA source, confint.mfrm_multivariate_d_study() returns exact F intervals for G and generalized confidence intervals for Phi (parm = "Phi") under independent normal random effects, using the source study's degrees of freedom at each requested future count. Phi includes Monte Carlo endpoint diagnostics and is not an exact-coverage method. Add reference = 1 for intervals on changes from the first plan: G maps the F set; Phi maps the generalized set and retains approximate coverage. Both include interior extrema; Phi differences retain joint numerical endpoint bands. These methods also apply to balanced nested plans when future child counts per parent equal the source count, using the parent count in the one-facet reduction. Complete balanced crossed two-facet sources default to approximate MLS null inversion for individual G/Phi intervals. Undefined MLS widths are conservatively retained and flagged by FormulaComplete; original estimates and numerical failures remain explicit. Small-source intervals may span almost all of [0,1]. These sources and general balanced nested plans also have explicitly selected experimental method = "approximate_f" and "mean_square_region" options for G/Phi; a vector requests both and plot() compares them. The confidence-interval help explains their assumptions, limitations and unavailable results. Use mfrm_multivariate_d_compare() separately for its supported paired-plan differences. For balanced or identifiable incomplete sources, explicit method = "reml_profile" fits approximate G/Phi or SEM intervals from the used ratings under normal effects. It retains original ANOVA/MINQUE estimates and reports the separate REML estimates as IntervalCenter. Numerical diagnostics and experimental finite-sample/boundary qualifications remain explicit; it is not a default. With reference, it supplies shared-profile interval images for one-facet or common-child nested plans, and direct difference profiles for other crossed/nested comparisons. The latter need optional nloptr and retain experimental calibration, especially at zero. SEM uses a direct error-variance profile followed by square roots; the numerical interval surrounds the REML center without enumerating remote disconnected accepted regions. Checked boundary populations showed below-nominal inclusion despite high numerical availability. Select parm = "RelativeSEM" or "AbsoluteSEM" for intervals on SEM itself from supported balanced crossed/nested sources. A single contributing mean square uses chi-square limits; otherwise MLS limits for the combined error variance are transformed by the square root. MLS coverage is approximate. One-facet SEM differences also accept reference = 1; nested MLS comparisons require a common future child count across plans. For one-facet RelativeSEM, explicit method = "residual_contrast" also accepts retained ANOVA/MINQUE ratings, including incomplete MINQUE sources. It transforms one residual chi-square interval and retains original points, a separate projected IntervalCenter, unavailable states and shared uncertainty across plans. Normal independent residuals and noninformative omissions are required; this does not supply AbsoluteSEM, G/Phi or multifacet intervals. Explicit method = "mean_square_region" supplies conservative individual SEM intervals and G/Phi/SEM difference enclosures for general balanced crossed/nested two-facet plans. The enclosure retains common source uncertainty but can be much wider than the tight difference image. plot(d, type = "sem", metric = "AbsoluteSEM", intervals = TRUE, assumption = "normal") adds the corresponding ribbon without refitting.

Calculation and interpretation limits

For crossed covariance component matrices P, R, T, PR, PT, RT, and E, universe-score covariance is P. Relative-error covariance is PR/n_r + PT/n_t + E/(n_r*n_t). Absolute-error covariance adds R/n_r + T/n_t + RT/(n_r*n_t). The G-study number of persons does not divide individual-score universe variance. Holding a count constant does not turn its random facet into a fixed facet. Composite weights define linear score combinations. They do not implement score-dependent panel trimming or an entire competition scoring rule. For a Person-by-Task G-study, E combines Person-by-Task interaction and within-cell error: relative-error covariance is E/n_t, absolute-error covariance is (T + E)/n_t, and universe-score covariance remains P. The same formulas apply to a Person-by-Rater design or to facets selected by facets, with names replaced in the declared order. For a single facet F and its planned count n, relative error is E/n and absolute error is (F + E)/n. A D-study cannot introduce an absent facet. For fixed tasks represented by score columns in a Person-by-Rater model, vary only Raters. The task set remains fixed, and each planned rater scores all tasks. See "Fixed tasks as score components" in mfrm_g_study() for the target and allocation requirements.

For raters nested within tasks, use the five components P, T, R(T), PT, and E, where E includes the Person-by-Rater-within-Task interaction. With n_r raters per task and n_t tasks, relative error is PT/n_t + E/(n_r*n_t); absolute error adds T/n_t + R(T)/(n_r*n_t). Universe covariance remains P. Other nested facet labels follow the same rules. All persons receive the same tasks and their nested raters; two raters per task at six tasks means twelve distinct raters, not two raters each judging six tasks. Future unequal child counts, changes of nesting are not supported. Nested G/Phi defaults and their differences require unchanged source child counts. Nested MLS SEM differences need a common future child count across plans, which may differ from the source. General nested coefficient intervals require explicit experimental methods; general difference enclosures use method = "mean_square_region". Individual nested SEM intervals allow both counts to change. See confint() above for the derivations and limitations.

For incomplete source data, counts of distinct observed levels are not per-person replication counts. This function projects a future complete design; it does not estimate the reliability of the observed sparse roster, heterogeneous person-specific assignments, or averages of them.

Each score uses diagonal entries; a composite uses w' Sigma w for each of the three covariance matrices. Thus between-score covariance affects composite dependability. G = UniverseVariance / (UniverseVariance + RelativeErrorVariance) and Phi uses absolute error instead. SEMs are square roots of the corresponding error variances, in the units of the score or specified composite of mean scores. Multiplying all weights by a nonzero constant multiplies SEMs by its absolute value but leaves G/Phi unchanged. Weights express a substantive choice; this function neither chooses them nor identifies an optimal design. Interpret a difference only when subtraction is meaningful on the supplied score scales. Comparing several composites holds the estimated components and planned designs constant, but different weights may change the construct being assessed. A higher coefficient alone does not justify that change. Compare SEMs across composites only when their scales are comparable.

The same weights define the universe-score composite and its observed mean-score estimate (the equal WWTS/AWTS case in mGENOVA). Different target and estimation weights, profile reliability, and accuracy at a cut score are not provided. Unlike mGENOVA's default D-study procedure, negative variance estimates are not replaced with zero by default. mGENOVA replaces negative variance components with zero for the D-study unless its NEGATIVE option is selected (manual, pages 15 and 21). That rule concerns variances, not all negative covariances, and does not guarantee PSD component matrices. Do not transfer that option's meaning to GENOVA 3.1 or jGENOVA: their NEGATIVE option controls printing of negative estimates. Their D-studies zero negative variances with either ALGORITHM or its default EMS convention; EMS also recalculates other components using the zero replacements. Matching a raw G-study estimate therefore need not give matching default D-studies. A matched negative-interaction example gives Phi = 0.73096 with the raw components retained here, 0.72727 in GENOVA 3.1 ALGORITHM, and 0.73532 with its default EMS. This is a component-treatment difference, not a coefficient-formula discrepancy. Select negative_components explicitly to reproduce either GENOVA D-study convention in supported univariate designs. EMS recalculation uses the source counts, before division by the future-plan counts. It is not REML or a positive-semidefinite matrix repair. Multivariate and MINQUE sources require "raw"; negative cross-score covariance is not a negative variance. GENOVA's NEGATIVE printing option is separate from this component-treatment choice.

gstudy retains raw estimates and diagnostics. effective_components contains the matrices actually used in projections; their diagnostics are in effective_component_diagnostics. ComponentTreatment identifies the choice in coefficient tables. ComponentPSD still describes the original G-study, so zero replacement does not erase evidence of problematic raw components. Save the complete result to preserve both sets. For GENOVA-adjusted results, confint() retains population-parameter intervals based on the original source study alongside adjusted points. IntervalEstimate records the original projection; bounds are not recentered on the adjusted Estimate. Any IntervalSE and other sampling diagnostics retain the original interval-method basis. Summary and plot methods accept intervals with the same recorded treatment. Supported population plan differences use confint(d, reference = ...); the separate delta-estimator comparison API still requires raw components. These intervals do not characterize the adjusted estimator's sampling law. See confint.mfrm_multivariate_d_study() for assumptions and distinctions.

Original covariance matrices and the selected projected variances remain available. G requires nonnegative universe and relative-error variances and a positive sum; Phi uses absolute-error variance instead. Each SEM requires only its corresponding nonnegative error variance. A failed requirement makes only that metric NA. Zero universe variance yields a coefficient of zero when its error variance is positive; a zero total variance leaves the coefficient undefined. Under "raw", no estimates are clipped or replaced.

Status summarizes a row as "Available", "Partially available", or "Unavailable"; the four metric-specific status columns give the reasons. ComponentPSD is TRUE only when all G-study component matrices pass their numerical PSD check. A FALSE value flags components for review without suppressing otherwise calculable projections. Print and plot methods display a note for non-PSD components. Calculability does not validate the joint covariance model or establish precise estimation; inspect component_diagnostics before interpreting estimates. Raw estimates can yield Phi > G when projected absolute error is less than relative error. Under the stated model, the extra absolute-error contributions are nonnegative; such a reversal calls for review of the estimated components, not a conclusion that absolute decisions are more dependable. Passing the matrix checks does not establish model fit. Outputs are point projections conditional on the estimated components, without confidence intervals, missing-data correction, or MFRM latent inference.

References

Brennan, R. L. (2001). Generalizability theory. Springer. Chapters 9–11. doi:10.1007/978-1-4757-3456-0 .

Brennan, R. L. (2001). Manual for mGENOVA, Version 2.1. Iowa Testing Programs Occasional Papers, No. 50. Pages 16 and 20–22; Appendices E and F, pages 74–81. Crick, J. E., and Brennan, R. L. (2021). Manual for jGENOVA, Version 1.0. Pages 2-10–2-11, 3-5, and A-22–A-23. Both manuals are available from the author's GENOVA Suite.

See also

plot.mfrm_multivariate_d_study(), mfrm_g_study(), mfrm_multivariate_d_compare(), mfrm_d_study()

Examples 

# Published synthetic two-score data: the same six tasks for ten persons.
tasks <- read.csv(system.file("extdata", "mgenova-table12.csv", package = "mfrmr"))
g <- mfrm_g_study(tasks, c("V", "W"), rater = NULL)

# Question: would doubling tasks improve the dependability of W minus V?
d <- mfrm_d_study(g, data.frame(Tasks = c(6, 12)),
  weights = c(V = -1, W = 1))
summary(d)
#>   Scenario Tasks      Kind     Score UniverseVariance RelativeErrorVariance
#> 1        1     6     Score         V       0.36814815             0.2087037
#> 2        1     6     Score         W       0.36888889             0.2561111
#> 3        1     6 Composite Composite       0.09851852             0.2298765
#> 4        2    12     Score         V       0.36814815             0.1043519
#> 5        2    12     Score         W       0.36888889             0.1280556
#> 6        2    12 Composite Composite       0.09851852             0.1149383
#>   AbsoluteErrorVariance         G       Phi RelativeSEM AbsoluteSEM    Status
#> 1             0.2661111 0.6382022 0.5804380   0.4568410   0.5158596 Available
#> 2             0.3094444 0.5902222 0.5438165   0.5060742   0.5562773 Available
#> 3             0.3100000 0.3000000 0.2411605   0.4794544   0.5567764 Available
#> 4             0.1330556 0.7791495 0.7345280   0.3230354   0.3647678 Available
#> 5             0.1547222 0.7423141 0.7045093   0.3578485   0.3933475 Available
#> 6             0.1550000 0.4615385 0.3886048   0.3390255   0.3937004 Available
#>     GStatus PhiStatus RelativeSEMStatus AbsoluteSEMStatus ComponentPSD
#> 1 Available Available         Available         Available         TRUE
#> 2 Available Available         Available         Available         TRUE
#> 3 Available Available         Available         Available         TRUE
#> 4 Available Available         Available         Available         TRUE
#> 5 Available Available         Available         Available         TRUE
#> 6 Available Available         Available         Available         TRUE
#>   ComponentTreatment
#> 1                raw
#> 2                raw
#> 3                raw
#> 4                raw
#> 5                raw
#> 6                raw
plot(d)

plot(d, type = "sem")

# G rises from 0.300 to 0.462, conditional on these estimated components.
# This is a planning projection, not evidence from twelve observed tasks.

# Without weights, report the original scores without creating a composite.
individual <- mfrm_d_study(g, data.frame(Tasks = c(6, 12)))
plot(individual, score = "V")


# Explicit GENOVA convention for a single observed score.
g_one <- mfrm_g_study(tasks, "V", rater = NULL)
d_ems <- mfrm_d_study(g_one, data.frame(Tasks = c(6, 12)),
  negative_components = "genova_ems")
summary(d_ems)
#>   Scenario Tasks  Kind Score UniverseVariance RelativeErrorVariance
#> 1        1     6 Score     V        0.3681481             0.2087037
#> 2        2    12 Score     V        0.3681481             0.1043519
#>   AbsoluteErrorVariance         G      Phi RelativeSEM AbsoluteSEM    Status
#> 1             0.2661111 0.6382022 0.580438   0.4568410   0.5158596 Available
#> 2             0.1330556 0.7791495 0.734528   0.3230354   0.3647678 Available
#>     GStatus PhiStatus RelativeSEMStatus AbsoluteSEMStatus ComponentPSD
#> 1 Available Available         Available         Available         TRUE
#> 2 Available Available         Available         Available         TRUE
#>   ComponentTreatment
#> 1         genova_ems
#> 2         genova_ems
ci_ems <- confint(d_ems, assumption = "normal")
# Adjusted point and original-source population interval have separate bases.
ci_ems[, c("Estimate", "IntervalEstimate", "Lower", "Upper", "IntervalBasis")]
#>    Estimate IntervalEstimate     Lower     Upper
#> 1 0.6382022        0.6382022 0.1272698 0.8962406
#> 2 0.7791495        0.7791495 0.2258018 0.9452815
#>                                 IntervalBasis
#> 1 Original source study; population parameter
#> 2 Original source study; population parameter
d_ems$effective_components # Compare with d_ems$gstudy$components.
#> $Person
#>           V
#> V 0.3681481
#> 
#> $Task
#>           V
#> V 0.3444444
#> 
#> $Residual
#>          V
#> V 1.252222
#> 
plot(d_ems, metric = "G", intervals = ci_ems) # Original-source population bounds.


# Compare weight choices on the same task-count scenarios.
weights <- cbind(Equal = c(V = 0.5, W = 0.5),
  W_focus = c(V = 0.2, W = 0.8), Difference = c(V = -1, W = 1))
alternatives <- mfrm_d_study(g,
  data.frame(Tasks = c(6, 12)), weights = weights)
summary(alternatives) # Original scores plus all three named composites.
